summary: Provides test vectors to validate implementations of the two mandatory authentication algorithm pairs of the TCP Authentication Option, over IPv4 and IPv6. They cover key derivation and message authentication codes, for whole segments and segments with options excluded. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Known right answers to check that your TCP security code does its math correctly.

subtitle: Reference answers to verify TCP-AO implementations work correctly.

tldr.problem: Implementing the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO) correctly is complex: the two mandatory algorithms involve key derivation and MAC computation with many edge cases, and implementers need concrete test cases to validate their code.
tldr.mechanism: This document provides test vectors—known input and output pairs—for both mandatory algorithm pairs (HMAC-SHA-1 and AES-128-CMAC) over both IPv4 and IPv6, covering multiple segment types and the variant where TCP options are excluded for middlebox compatibility.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can now validate their TCP-AO code against these vectors to catch bugs in key derivation, MAC computation, header coverage, and other common pitfalls before deployment.

today: RFC 9235 is an Informational RFC published in May 2022. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the definitive source of test vectors for TCP-AO implementations and is widely used to validate cryptographic correctness in both open-source and commercial TCP stacks.

sections.title: What TCP-AO Is and Why Test Vectors Matter
sections.content:
TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO) is a mechanism that lets TCP endpoints authenticate each other and ensure TCP segments have not been altered in flight. It is defined in RFC 5925. The actual cryptography is specified in RFC 5926, which mandates two algorithm pairs: KDF_HMAC_SHA1 with HMAC-SHA-1-96, and KDF_AES_128_CMAC with AES-128-CMAC-96.

TCP-AO involves multiple steps: deriving traffic keys from a master key, computing a MAC over the TCP segment (with or without options), and placing that MAC in the TCP-AO option. Many implementers make mistakes in these steps. This document provides test vectors—concrete examples with known correct answers—so implementers can verify their code before shipping.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP-AO is a way to sign TCP messages so the receiver knows they came from who they claim to be. This RFC gives you the correct signatures for test messages.

sections.title: The Test Setup and Parameters
sections.content:
All test vectors use a single master key: the ASCII string "testvector" (10 bytes). The test connection uses specific IP addresses (10.11.12.13 for IPv4 client, 172.27.28.29 for server; fd00::1 and fd00::2 for IPv6), and both sides use different KeyIDs: 0x3d (61) for the client and 0x54 (84) for the server.

The test segments include standard TCP options in a defined order: Maximum Segment Size (MSS), No Operation (NOP), Window Scale, Selective Acknowledgment (SACK) permitted, and Timestamp. Some vectors show the MAC with options covered; others exclude the options from the MAC calculation to test middlebox traversal compatibility. All packets use aggressive TTL/hop limit (255) and DSCP CS7 (typical for BGP), but no IP options.
sections.plainLanguage: The tests use made-up IP addresses and a secret word. They check both the normal case and a special case where the receiver ignores some TCP options.

sections.title: What the Test Vectors Cover
sections.content:
The vectors are organized by protocol version and algorithm. For each combination (IPv4 or IPv6, and KDF_HMAC_SHA1 or KDF_AES_128_CMAC), there are test vectors for sending and receiving, both with and without TCP options covered by the MAC. Each vector includes the traffic key (derived from the master key), the complete IPv4/TCP or IPv6/TCP packet, and the correct MAC value.

The document specifies traffic in both directions: client sending SYN, server responding with SYN-ACK, and both sides sending regular data segments. This exercises different segment types and ensures the key derivation is correct at each step. Additionally, the document lists common implementation errors: mistakes in algorithm selection, incorrect handling of the pseudo-header, string encoding bugs, and header coverage issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The vectors test both directions of a conversation, both types of algorithms, and both ways of computing the MAC. They are organized so you can test one piece at a time.

sections.title: How to Use These Vectors in Practice
sections.content:
An implementation should extract each test vector and feed it through its key derivation function (KDF) to compute the traffic key. Then it should compute the MAC over the specified packet data (with or without TCP options as indicated) using the derived traffic key and the specified algorithm. The computed MAC must match the expected MAC byte-for-byte.

These test vectors were generated by multiple independent implementations and validated against each other for interoperability. They include test cases that often trip up implementers: zero-initialized fields that must be computed correctly, handling of the pseudo-header from the IP layer, sequence number boundary conditions, and the nuances of the two mandatory algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: Run your code on each test case. If your MAC matches the expected MAC, your code is probably right.

sections.title: Observed Common Mistakes
sections.content:
The RFC documents five categories of common implementation errors. Algorithm issues include confusion about which KDF goes with which MAC algorithm, or using the wrong field names when building the pseudo-header. Algorithm parameters include mistakes in truncating the MAC output to 96 bits, or computing CMAC incorrectly. String handling includes bugs in byte order or padding.

Header coverage issues are the trickiest: some implementations incorrectly handle the case where the TCP checksum field must be zeroed during MAC computation, or they cover the wrong TCP options. The document notes that both whole-segment and options-excluded test vectors are provided precisely because this is a common error point.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementers often mess up: getting the algorithm names mixed up, forgetting to zero some fields, byte ordering, and deciding wrong about which parts of the segment to include in the signature.
